task.name: A phase allowance is derived without reference to the story ceiling that bounds it, and waiting for an operator counts as worker unresponsiveness, so converging stories are failed on wall clock
task.story_text:
## Observed

Three of six stories in one sprint failed on the worker timeout. None failed on quality. Together
they accounted for roughly 70% of the sprint's spend, and every one of them was doing legitimate work
or legitimately waiting when it was killed.

Two distinct shapes produced the same outcome.

A story sat at an operator decision gate. Eighteen seconds before it was killed, the run logged that
the gate still had 41 minutes 54 seconds remaining. The worker timeout counted the time spent waiting
for an operator as time the worker was unresponsive, so the wait the system had itself chosen to
begin was charged against the story as a fault. The gate's own wait was configured equal to the base
worker timeout, so on any story taking that base value the gate could not have been answered in time
by anyone, and the decision it asked for could never have been supplied.

Separately, a story running to the larger complexity-derived worker ceiling was allotted a
per-invocation development timeout equal to roughly 92% of that whole-story ceiling. It ran three
development cycles and two review cycles inside a budget sized for barely one, and was killed by
signal mid-edit on the third. Its reviews had been converging — the finding count had narrowed
between cycles — and its accumulated work was preserved, so the failure records a wall-clock ceiling
rather than a verdict on the change. The killed invocation also reported no measurable cost, so the
story's spend is unknown.

## Expected

An allowance derived for one part of a unit of work is derived against the budget that contains it,
so a phase cannot be granted more time than the story enclosing it can spend, and a story cannot be
granted a per-cycle allowance it can only use by having a single cycle. Where several cycles are
possible, the allowances remain consistent with the enclosing ceiling across every count of cycles
that can actually occur, not only the smallest.

Time spent waiting for a decision the system has asked a human to make is not time the worker is
unresponsive. A unit of work is not failed for the duration of a wait the system chose to begin, and
a deadline that would elapse during such a wait either accounts for the wait or is extended by it.

Where a deadline is nonetheless reached, the outcome distinguishes a unit that exhausted its time
from one that produced a wrong or unacceptable result, because the two call for different operator
actions and only one of them is evidence about the work.

## Diagnosis

**Observed symptom.** Stories are failed with a timeout outcome while converging or while waiting at a gate,
and the recorded failure is indistinguishable in kind from a quality failure.

**Evidence.**

- Run log, gate-waiting story: `Waiting for pending decision on <id> (41m 54s remaining)` at one
  timestamp, then `TIMEOUT <story> (worker unresponsive after 3600s — marking as failed)` eighteen
  seconds later.
- Same run: that story's worker timeout was reported as the base default, and the gate's configured
  wait equalled it, so gate expiry necessarily fell outside the worker window.
- Run log, converging story: worker timeout reported at the larger complexity-derived value; the
  per-invocation development timeout reported at roughly 92% of it; three development cycles
  attempted; final invocation ended by signal with no measurable cost recorded.
- `docs/guides/inputs-reference.md:82` — the worker timeout is configurable and unset in this
  project, so both stories took derived values.

**Ruled out.** Not agent quality: one story's findings narrowed across review cycles and the other
was not reviewed at all before being killed. Not the preservation path, which worked — both
workspaces were preserved and one checkpoint-committed stranded work. Not a hung worker: the
gate-waiting story was polling normally and logging remaining time, and the other was mid-edit.

**Confirmed cause.** Phase-level and gate-level allowances are derived independently of the
whole-story ceiling that bounds them, and the whole-story ceiling measures elapsed wall clock without
excluding intervals in which the system is deliberately waiting on an operator.

**Affected code path.** Worker timeout derivation and enforcement in the sprint runner, the
complexity-derived per-invocation development timeout, and the pending-decision wait.

**Fix-success criterion.** A story that reaches an operator gate can have that gate answered within
its own deadline; a story permitted more than one development cycle can complete them within its
ceiling; and a timeout outcome is recorded distinguishably from a quality failure.

handoff.summary: Made the sprint worker timeout the enclosing budget for everything inside a story, and stopped charging operator waits against it. A new stdlib-only leaf module (src/theforge/worker_budget.py) lets the sprint runner publish each dispatched story's ceiling — keyed by the thread-local worker slug log_util already owns, so no signatures change and it no-ops under standalone `forge run` — and holds the operator-wait ledger. coordinator/util.py gained cap_timeout_to_story_ceiling (static: fit the invocations one review cycle may run inside the ceiling, with an audited floor) and clamp_timeout_to_remaining (dynamic: never grant an invocation more than the story's remaining working time); both are applied at seating in engine.py, at the dev_phase dispatch site including its previously-uncapped `or _resolved_timeout` fallback, and on the timeout-escalation path that re-derived from the profile base. pending.poll_pending now wraps its whole poll in an operator-wait interval and bounds the requested wait against the remaining story budget; all three gates (human review, plan review, escalate) compute the bounded window before write_pending so the operator-visible timeout_at matches what the poller honours. The scheduler credits accrued and in-flight operator waits back to the story deadline before its expiry check, for both single-story and batch dispatch (batch members share one budget group since one thread serves them all). Timeout outcomes keep ABNORMAL_WORKER_TIMEOUT and now state deadline exhaustion, name any excluded wait, and no longer say 'worker unresponsive'. Recording the clamps in the audit required a record schema bump to v26 with a migration helper and regenerated fixture.

handoff.summary: Iteration 5 fixed the batch-group P1. WorkerBudget.remaining() offset elapsed clock with the member's own operator-wait ledger while the scheduler's _effective_deadline credited the whole group's, so in a cost-aware batch a member reaching a gate after a peer had waited computed against elapsed clock that included the peer's wait but credited none of it back — and was offered no pending-decision wait on a story whose deadline had not moved. Grouped members share one started_at, ceiling and deadline, so the offset is now shared too: a new WorkerBudget.pooled_credit() is what remaining() subtracts, and it is the same number _effective_deadline adds, so the scheduler's deadline and every allowance derived inside the story come from one figure. Ungrouped stories are their own only peer, leaving the single-story path arithmetically unchanged. Swept every consumer rather than the cited line: remaining(), operator_wait_credit() and the seconds operator_wait() yields all read pooled_credit, so both timeout clamps (pending.bounded_gate_wait and dev dispatch's clamp_timeout_to_remaining, both of which reach it via remaining()) and remaining_seconds() are covered; waiting_on_operator already scanned peers; and _group_peers now includes the budget itself when the registry no longer holds it, so a member unregistered at completion still accounts for its own ledger. Collateral audit of the earlier commits: the runner reads operator_wait_credit before unregistering on the expiry path so the timeout message still reports the group's excluded wait, and no lock is held across another acquisition so pooling adds no deadlock. finding_registry.description: When a development invocation is dispatched with less than 60 seconds of story working time left, it receives a 60 second timeout that can outlive the story deadline.
Existing tests still assert the old timeout wording 'Worker timeout' and 'Worker thread timed out after', so they no longer reflect the new deadline-exhaustion language emitted by the sprint runner.

In a cost-aware batch group, after one member spends time at an operator gate, a later member can be offered no pending-decision wait even though the shared story deadline still has credited working time.

Gate waits are bounded twice, once in pending_hitl before write_pending and again inside poll_pending, so the pending file's timeout_at can advertise a longer window than the poller actually honors, causing an operator-facing gate to expire and be cleaned up before the advertised deadline.

The human-review and plan-review gates bound the operator wait once before write_pending but then poll for the full pre-bounded window with already_bounded=True, so an operator answering during the write+notify interval can hit a poller that has already returned timeout and swept the checkpoint even though the advertised timeout_at has not been reached.

soft: Coordinator is pure Python — no LLM calls for routing or process decisions
Schema validation is the integrity boundary — do not relax cross-validation rules

Keep modules single-purpose. Extract when a responsibility separates from its neighbours — never to satisfy a line count. Putting a change in an already-large module is correct if that is where it belongs; a module carved at whatever line got the count down is worse than the large module it came from.
Keep pure-data types in low-dependency modules with stdlib-only imports
Separate prompt construction, output parsing, and coordinator control flow

When adding or modifying data that flows between coordinator phases, instrument the change so the actual values are visible in the audit trail — diagnosing sprint failures requires tracing real data, not reconstructing it
Do not create files outside src/, tests/, or docs/. If you need a scratch file for exploration, delete it before committing.

Changes that affect coordinator phase boundaries, state handoff between phases, or adaptive routing/config propagation must include seam-level integration tests covering the touched boundary. Unit tests alone are insufficient when correctness depends on cross-phase state flow.
